title: Umutsha (belt)
region: Zulu or Sotho peoples, South Africa
altText: A long, narrow band of beadwork, about 72 centimeters long and under 4 centimeters wide, made of small glass beads. It is a belt meant to be worn around the waist.

context: A beaded belt called an umutsha, made by a Zulu or Sotho artist in South Africa. The record dates it to the 19th or 20th century and lists leather, glass beads, cloth, and fiber. It is about 72 centimeters long and under 4 centimeters wide. Glass beads in southern Africa were largely imported, and beadwork was made into many kinds of clothing and jewelry.

descriptions.k: This is a long, thin belt made of tiny beads. It was made in South Africa. Someone sewed many, many beads, one by one. Can you find a pattern in the beads? What colors do you see?
descriptions.g12: This long, thin belt is made of tiny glass beads. An artist in South Africa made it by sewing the beads, one at a time. The beads make patterns. Look for lines, zigzags, and shapes. Which pattern do you notice first?
descriptions.g35: This belt is called an umutsha. A Zulu or Sotho artist in South Africa sewed tiny glass beads onto it in patterns. It is a very long, narrow band, about 72 centimeters long, so a close look will show many small shapes. Beadwork takes patience, because each bead is placed by hand. How do the patterns work together along the whole belt?
descriptions.g68: Beadwork in southern Africa developed using glass beads brought by trade, and artists used them to make belts, necklaces, and other adornments in many styles. This umutsha is long and narrow, so its patterns have to work as a band that repeats and changes along its length. The record lists glass beads with leather, cloth, and fiber. Some writers describe bead colors and patterns as carrying messages, but scholars caution that meanings varied by place, maker, and time. How do you read patterns without assuming a code?
descriptions.g910: This umutsha shows how beadwork turns a long, narrow band into a field for design. Glass beads were imported into southern Africa, and artists used them to create distinctive local styles, which vary by region and community. The attribution here is to a Zulu or Sotho artist, which reflects uncertainty about the maker's community. Popular accounts claim that colors and patterns spell out messages, yet researchers warn that this can oversimplify, because meanings depend on context. How does the form of the band shape the way patterns are arranged?
descriptions.g1112: A beaded belt like this invites two kinds of attention: close attention to the work of arranging thousands of small beads into pattern, and caution about claims regarding what the pattern means. Southern African beadwork became a visible art form with imported glass beads, and styles differ by region, community, and period; the museum attributes this one only to a Zulu or Sotho artist. Popular claims that bead colors form a fixed code have been challenged because meaning is local and changes. How can a viewer appreciate design while respecting the limits of what the object reveals?

teacherNote.context: A beaded belt (umutsha) attributed to a Zulu or Sotho artist, South Africa, 19th to 20th century. Avoid claiming that bead colors have a single fixed meaning; scholars note that meanings vary by place, maker, and time.
directions: Have students design a bead pattern on grid paper for a long, narrow band, using repetition and one deliberate change.
Discuss the idea of patterns that mean something to a community, and how outsiders should approach them respectfully.
Trace the path of glass beads in trade using a world map, and discuss how objects and ideas travel.
